target.title: Online speech synthesis using a chronically implanted brain–computer interface in an individual with ALS
target.version: Version of Record, Scientific Reports 14:9617, published online 2024-04-26 (wiki text: PMC11053081 BioC XML); first public as medRxiv preprint 10.1101/2023.06.30.23291352 v1, posted 2023-07-01 (only version; Crossref has-preprint relation confirms)

read.pdf: Figs. 1–4; no tables; full reference list

version_check.wiki_source: published article full text (PMC11053081), sha256 8e40f0bf78bed0c908d8b39a10ecb765fb4f3de9edcda571028e47c26ef41fc9, text_sha256 da890c37530a2660548dbeaa1e46c2a40aa91e831327bc62f20ad9d8412818aa

entries.text: Authors present a closed-loop, online ECoG speech-synthesis proof of concept in one ALS clinical-trial participant with impaired articulation.
entries.condition: Chronically implanted intracranial ECoG; overt speech production; single participant.
entries.quote: Here, a participant with impaired articulation and phonation was able to use a chronically implanted investigational device to produce acoustic speech that retained his unique voice characteristics.

entries.text: Three recurrent-network stages identify speech, map neural sequences to acoustic features, and synthesize the waveform.
entries.condition: Online pipeline: unidirectional nVAD, bidirectional acoustic decoder, and LPCNet vocoder.

entries.text: The BCI participant was one male native English speaker in his 60s with ALS and impaired articulation; isolated words remained intelligible while continuous speech was mostly unintelligible.
entries.condition: Single male native English speaker with ALS; no additional BCI speakers were evaluated.

entries.text: At implantation, the participant had been diagnosed with ALS 8 years earlier and scored 26/48 on ALSFRS-R, with speech rated 1 point.
entries.unit: years since diagnosis; ALSFRS-R total points; speech subscore points
entries.condition: One participant, measured in the clinical-trial participant description; speech subscore is part of the 48-point ALSFRS-R.

entries.text: The participant had 128 subdural ECoG electrodes arranged in two 8 × 8 grids.
entries.condition: Chronic subdural ECoG implant; grids covered left-hemisphere speech sensorimotor and upper-extremity areas.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Study device and implantation

entries.text: The analysis and online synthesizer used a subset of 64 electrodes selected for speech-related high-gamma activity.
entries.condition: Subset from the two-grid chronic ECoG implant; selected channels span motor, premotor, and somatosensory areas including dorsal laryngeal area.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Signal processing and feature extraction; Fig. 1

entries.text: Neural signals were acquired at 1000 Hz.
entries.condition: Neuroport ECoG acquisition during training and testing sessions.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Data recording

entries.text: Broadband high-gamma features covered 70–170 Hz; the first line-noise harmonic at 118–122 Hz was attenuated.
entries.unit: Hz feature band; Hz attenuated band
entries.condition: Log-power features from ECoG after common-average referencing and channel selection.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Signal processing and feature extraction

entries.text: Neural features were logarithmic power using 50 ms windows and 10 ms frameshifts; acoustic recordings were downsampled from 48 kHz to 16 kHz and padded by 16 ms for filter delay.
entries.unit: ms window; ms frameshift; kHz input audio; kHz resampled audio; ms padding
entries.condition: Feature extraction and target-audio alignment for training and evaluation.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Signal processing and feature extraction

entries.text: The bidirectional decoder predicted 18 Bark-scale cepstral coefficients and 2 pitch parameters for LPCNet synthesis.
entries.condition: Frame-wise acoustic target representation decoded from each detected speech segment.

entries.text: The closed vocabulary contained six communication-board keywords: Left, Right, Up, Down, Enter, and Back; silence was also prompted.
entries.condition: Overt, self-paced word production for communication-board control; this is a closed-vocabulary task, not open-set speech.
entries.quote: Here, we focused on a closed vocabulary of 6 keywords, originally used for decoding spoken commands to control a communication board.
entries.loc: Sec. Introduction; Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design

entries.text: Training prompts were read aloud, with 10 repetitions of each keyword per block (60 word trials), 2 s per prompt and a 3 s intertrial interval; at least 1 s separated the end of speech from the next trial.
entries.unit: repetitions per word; words per block; s prompt; s intertrial interval; s minimum post-speech gap
entries.condition: Single participant; fixed-seed pseudo-randomized order; occasional silence trials.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design

entries.text: Training recordings were collected over 6 weeks; training, validation, and test data came from 10 recording days.
entries.condition: All data came from the same ALS participant; partitions were assigned by recording day.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design

entries.text: The training partition comprised 1570 trials and approximately 80 min of data, including 21.8 min of pure speech.
entries.unit: trials; min total; min pure speech
entries.condition: Training partition in the single-participant keyword-reading dataset; recording days separated from validation and test days.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design

entries.text: Validation and test partitions each contained 70 trials, approximately 3 min total and 0.9 min of pure speech.
entries.unit: trials per partition; min total per partition; min pure speech per partition
entries.condition: Validation and test sets were collected on different days from training and from each other.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design

entries.text: Partitions were separated by recording day; validation data selected hyperparameters, while the held-out test set was used to assess generalizability before online sessions and for saliency analysis.
entries.condition: Different days, but the same participant/speaker across training, validation, test, and online deployment.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design

entries.text: Each recording day began with syllable repetitions used to calculate day-specific channel means and standard deviations for high-gamma feature normalization.
entries.condition: Separate baseline statistics per recording day; the paper states that training statistics did not leak into validation or test.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design; Signal processing and feature extraction

entries.text: The baseline task used 12 consonant–vowel syllables, each repeated 5 times; each stimulus lasted 1 s and trial duration varied from 2.5 to 3.5 s in 80 ms steps.
entries.unit: syllables; repetitions each; s stimulus; s trial range; ms step
entries.condition: Same-day syllable-repetition calibration recordings; high-gamma mean and standard deviation computed per channel.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design

entries.text: The unidirectional nVAD used two LSTM layers with 150 units each and a two-class output for speech versus non-speech.
entries.condition: nVAD training on frame-wise speech/non-speech labels from overt-speech recordings.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Network architectures

entries.text: nVAD used truncated BPTT with k1=50 and k2=100 frames, limiting backpropagation to 1 s and repeating updates every 500 ms.
entries.unit: frames k1; frames k2; s backpropagation span; ms update interval
entries.condition: High-gamma frames at 10 ms frameshift; training on keyword and silence trials.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Network architectures

entries.text: Both recurrent models used 50% dropout and RMSprop-adjusted stochastic-gradient-descent learning rates initialized at 0.001; validation performance controlled checkpoint updates.
entries.condition: nVAD checkpoint by validation frame accuracy; decoder checkpoint by validation loss.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Network architectures

entries.text: The nVAD was trained for 27,975 update steps and reached 93.4% frame-wise accuracy on held-out validation data.
entries.condition: nVAD binary speech/non-speech frame classification; selected/held-out validation partition.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Network architectures

entries.text: The nVAD architecture had 311,102 trainable weights.
entries.condition: Unidirectional two-layer LSTM nVAD.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Network architectures

entries.text: The bidirectional decoder used two bidirectional LSTM layers with 100 units per layer and a 20-dimensional output (18 cepstral coefficients plus 2 pitch parameters).
entries.unit: LSTM layers × units; acoustic output dimensions
entries.condition: Sequence regression on nVAD-extracted overt-speech segments; future and past context available.
entries.quote: The network architecture of the bidirectional decoding model had a very similar configuration to the unidirectional nVAD but employed a stack of bidirectional LSTM layers for sequence modelling
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Network architectures; Fig. 4

entries.text: The bidirectional decoder had 378,420 trainable weights and was trained for 14,130 update steps.
entries.condition: Decoder trained on utterance-aligned high-gamma and LPC-feature sequences; validation loss used for best-model selection.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Network architectures

entries.text: The headline intelligibility result was 80% listener accuracy for synthesized words from the closed six-keyword vocabulary.
entries.condition: 21 native English listeners; synthesized samples from 3 closed-loop sessions; six forced-choice keyword options; 2 no-output samples and some silent false detections were excluded.
entries.quote: Overall, human listeners achieved an accuracy score of 80%, indicating that the majority of synthesized words could be correctly and reliably recognized.

entries.text: The listening test included 180 samples; 2 words without detected speech activity and hence without synthesized output were excluded.
entries.condition: Listener intelligibility test using words produced during the 3 closed-loop sessions; additional false nVAD detections yielding silence were also excluded.
entries.quote: Out of 180 samples, we excluded 2 words because the nVAD model did not detect speech activity and therefore no speech output was produced by the decoding model.

entries.text: A few additional nVAD false detections produced synthesized silence that the participant did not notice; the paper does not quantify these cases.
entries.condition: Online closed-loop word production and listener sample selection.
entries.quote: We also excluded a few cases where speech activity was falsely detected by the nVAD model, which resulted in synthesized silence and remained unnoticed to the participant.

entries.text: The decoder produced an intelligible but incorrect word in 4% of cases; listeners correctly recognized that incorrect output.
entries.condition: Synthesized keyword samples in the closed-vocabulary listener test; the incorrect output was acoustically intelligible to listeners.

entries.text: Individual listener accuracies for synthesized words ranged from 75% to 84%.
entries.condition: All listeners in the 21-person native-English listening panel; synthesized samples only; chance was 16.7%.

entries.text: The six-choice listening test had a stated chance level of 16.7%; every listener scored above it.
entries.condition: Six forced-choice keyword labels; chance is 1/6; comparison is per-listener synthesized-word accuracy.
entries.quote: All human listeners achieved accuracy scores above chance (16.7%).

entries.text: Listeners recognized 99.8% of the participant’s original spoken keyword samples.
entries.condition: Natural, overtly spoken samples from the same six keywords, evaluated by the listening-test panel.

entries.text: Figure 2C’s diagonal listener-recognition rates were Left 96.0%, Right 83.8%, Up 95.7%, Down 86.8%, Enter 78.6%, and Back 37.3%.
entries.value: Left 96.0; Right 83.8; Up 95.7; Down 86.8; Enter 78.6; Back 37.3
entries.condition: Confusion matrix over synthesized samples only; entries are the diagonal percentages for human choices matching ground truth; see Fig. 2C.
entries.quote: The confusion matrix shows that human listeners were able to recognize all but one word at very high rates.

entries.text: Back was least intelligible and was often confused with Left; the authors attribute this partly to close vowel-formant proximity and weak tongue movements.
entries.condition: Closed six-keyword vocabulary; qualitative explanation of Back/Left listener confusions.

entries.text: Median Levenshtein distance between spoken and synthesized voice-activity sequences was 235 ms.
entries.condition: Timing comparison of participant-spoken and synthesized speech activity in the online keyword task.

entries.text: Mean original-versus-synthesized spectral correlation was 0.67 with standard deviation 0.18.
entries.condition: Per-sample correlation averaged across 80 mel-scaled spectral bins after STFT, Hanning windowing, and natural-log transform; speech waveforms were time-aligned.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Synthesis performance; Sec. Statistical analysis

entries.text: Online evaluation comprised 3 sessions on 3 different days, approximately 5.5 months after training; each lasted 6 min.
entries.unit: sessions; days; months post-training; min per session
entries.condition: Closed-loop online keyword task with acoustic feedback; other experiment parameters were unchanged.
entries.quote: We conducted 3 sessions across 3 different days (approximately 5 and a half months after the training data was acquired, each session lasted 6 min)

entries.text: Synthesized audio was played only after the participant finished the same prompted word, avoiding simultaneous feedback during speech production.
entries.condition: Delayed auditory feedback after each utterance; bidirectional decoding requires the full segment.
entries.quote: The feedback from each synthesized word began after he spoke the same word, avoiding any interference with production from the acoustic feedback.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design

entries.text: Across the 3 later sessions, the model was recalibrated but not retrained in each session.
entries.condition: Training data preceded online testing by approximately 5.5 months; day-specific normalization was recalibrated for online use.

entries.text: Authors argue that similar performance after a five-and-a-half-month gap supports ECoG stability for speech synthesis, but explicitly call for longer longitudinal testing.
entries.condition: One participant; 3 separate test days; recalibration without retraining; no longer-term follow-up reported here.

entries.text: Authors claim that online synthesis retained voice and pacing characteristics and could produce intelligible commands at the participant’s own pace.
entries.condition: Subject-specific acoustic targets learned from overt speech; listening recognition and speech-spectrum similarity assessed in a six-keyword task.

entries.text: The model did not synthesize unseen words; it learned word-specific neural dynamics rather than syllable- or phoneme-level units.
entries.condition: Closed six-word training and evaluation vocabulary; open-vocabulary generalization was not tested.
entries.quote: While our results are promising, the approach used here did not allow for synthesis of unseen words.

entries.text: Training required neural data during overt speech, limiting the current method to people who can still vocalize and may need speech that remains intelligible.
entries.condition: Ground-truth acoustic speech was available and time-aligned; silent speech and anarthria were not demonstrated.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that the demonstration avoided the absent-ground-truth problem; voice-banking or generic-voice alternatives would require careful alignment or lose individual voice characteristics.
entries.condition: Overt speech and aligned acoustic targets were available for training and evaluation.

entries.text: The authors do not know how long intelligible output will persist as ALS changes neural responses and articulatory function.
entries.condition: Longitudinal follow-up beyond the observed post-training interval is required.

entries.text: Bidirectional decoding imposed a delay until the participant finished speaking each word; the authors considered this acceptable and potentially useful for progressive speech impairment.
entries.condition: Delayed word-level acoustic feedback; no quantitative end-to-end latency is reported.
entries.quote: the bidirectional LSTM imposed a delay in the audible feedback until after the patient spoke each word.

entries.text: Saliency analysis highlighted nVAD influence from 300 to 100 ms before predicted speech onset.
entries.condition: High-gamma feature contributions to the nVAD speech-onset decision; interpretation based on test-set saliency analysis.
entries.loc: Fig. 3A; Sec. Results, Anatomical and temporal contributions

entries.text: Figure 3C plots 3 selected channels over 1 s before predicted speech onset, with N=60 saliency observations.
entries.condition: Mean absolute relevance scores; shading is standard error; test-set saliency analysis.
entries.loc: Fig. 3C; Sec. Results, Anatomical and temporal contributions

entries.text: Saliency analysis attributes most nVAD speech-onset information to motor, premotor, and somatosensory areas; dorsal laryngeal electrodes contributed only modestly.
entries.condition: Model-gradient saliency for predicted speech onsets, not a causal stimulation test.
entries.loc: Sec. Results, Anatomical and temporal contributions; Fig. 3

entries.text: The listening test used a forced-choice selection among six labels; listeners could replay each sample many times, and sample order was independently randomized across listeners.
entries.condition: 21 native English listeners; samples from all 3 online sessions; both synthesized and original participant speech included.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Listening test

entries.text: The listening panel comprised 21 native English speakers aged 18–30; 23.8% identified as male, 61.9% as female, and 14% as other or preferred not to answer.
entries.unit: listeners; years; % male; % female; % other/no response
entries.condition: Anonymous demographics collected after the forced-choice listening test; recruitment was indirect and participants had no direct connection to the PI.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Listening test

entries.text: Spectral correlation used Pearson coefficients across 80 mel-scaled bins from log-transformed STFTs with 50 ms Hanning windows and 10 ms frameshifts; correlations were averaged across bins.
entries.unit: mel bins; ms window; ms frameshift
entries.condition: Original versus reconstructed speech spectrograms; sample-level Pearson correlation averaged over frequency bins.

entries.text: Feature-selection confidence intervals were two-sided 95%; contamination tests used Bonferroni-corrected alpha 0.05/N.
entries.condition: Feature selection across time points; N is frequency bins multiplied by selected channels for contamination testing.

entries.text: Contamination analysis identified one likely contaminated channel on 3 recording days; the channel was replaced by neighboring-channel averages, and authors concluded residual acoustic contamination was absent.
entries.unit: channel; recording days; neighbors in correction
entries.condition: Channel 46 contaminated on D5–D7; corrected using an 8-neighbor configuration excluding bad channel 38.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Contamination analysis

entries.text: The target paper cites a prior single-person ALS locked-in case in which a fully implanted ECoG BCI provided a stable spelling switch for more than 3 years.
entries.condition: Prior patient with locked-in syndrome due to ALS; stable switch control for a spelling application, not speech synthesis.

entries.text: The target paper cites robust speech-auditory-cortex ECoG responses in two drug-resistant epilepsy patients over 1.5 years.
entries.condition: Prior chronic ambulatory ECoG study in drug-resistant epilepsy; signal-response stability, not speech synthesis performance.

entries.text: The paper does not report the exact count of additional false nVAD detections/silent outputs or the final number of scored synthesized samples after exclusions.
entries.condition: 80% accuracy is reported after excluding 2 no-output words and an unquantified few false-detection cases.
entries.quote: We also excluded a few cases where speech activity was falsely detected by the nVAD model, which resulted in synthesized silence and remained unnoticed to the participant.

entries.text: The paper does not report a neural-network training random seed or number of independent training runs; the fixed seeds mentioned apply to prompted-word order only.
entries.condition: Training uses stochastic optimizers and shuffled data loaders; linked scripts contain no explicit RNG seed initialization.
entries.loc: Sec. Materials and methods, Experiment recordings and task design; train_unidirectional_vad.py:64-109; train_bidirectional_model.py:36-105

entries.text: The paper gives the chance level and listener-level accuracy range but does not state a confidence interval or uncertainty estimate for the 80% headline listener-recognition accuracy.
entries.condition: Closed six-choice listener test; SD/CI reported for spectral correlation, not for word-recognition accuracy.
entries.quote: Overall, human listeners achieved an accuracy score of 80%, indicating that the majority of synthesized words could be correctly and reliably recognized.

entries.text: No quantitative head-to-head comparison with another decoder or speech-synthesis system is reported; superiority is not established by a comparative benchmark.
entries.condition: Authors report a proof of concept and single-system performance on a closed-vocabulary task.

entries.text: The paper describes LPCNet waveform synthesis but no language model or linguistic post-decoding aid; outputs were evaluated within a six-keyword task.
entries.condition: No external LM or lexicon-based correction is described; closed vocabulary derives from task prompts, not an LM-assisted decoder.

entries.text: The repository replication script sets the decoder and nVAD test day to 2022-11-03 and validation day to 2022-11-04; the paper states only that partitions were on separate days.
entries.condition: Both training commands in the replication script use those dates; training data comprise the remaining days.

entries.text: The training-script defaults reverse the replication-script split: default test day 2022-11-04 and validation day 2022-11-03.
entries.unit: default test day; default validation day
entries.condition: Defaults in both training scripts differ from the dates passed by replicate.sh; exact split used for the published weights is not resolved by paper text alone.

entries.text: The repository README says confidence-interval statistics used to identify speech-information channels were computed only on training data.
entries.condition: Selection statistics based on the recorded speech data; channel selection excluded the held-out validation and test partitions.

entries.text: Corpus preparation amplitude-normalizes each non-silence audio segment and applies a default −3 dB gain before extracting LPC/VAD targets; this audio-level normalization is not stated in the paper text.
entries.condition: Applied to non-silence training speech segments before LPC feature and energy-VAD extraction; silence is not normalized this way.

entries.text: The replication script trains nVAD for 8 epochs and the bidirectional decoder for 20 epochs; paper text reports update steps but not epoch counts.
entries.unit: epochs for nVAD; epochs for decoder
entries.condition: Values passed by replicate.sh, not the training-script decoder default of 100 epochs.

entries.text: The bidirectional training script synthesizes and saves up to 30 held-out test trials after each epoch for preview; checkpoint selection itself uses validation loss.
entries.condition: Test examples are used for epochwise qualitative outputs during training, while best weights are chosen by held-out validation loss.

entries.text: The repository training loaders shuffle training data, and the source has no explicit RNG seed initialization, so repeated model fits are not pinned to a reported seed.
entries.condition: nVAD and decoder training use shuffled DataLoaders; no explicit random, NumPy, or Torch seed-setting call appears in the training scripts.

entries.text: Authors infer that the neural-acoustic correspondence did not change significantly over the 5.5-month interval.
entries.condition: No statistical comparison with an earlier test is reported; inference from post-gap sessions only.
entries.quote: These findings suggest that the correspondence between neural activity in ventral sensorimotor cortex and speech acoustics were not significantly changed over this time period.

entries.text: Authors state that the 3 test days produced similar results with recalibration but no retraining, using training data from 5.5 months earlier.
entries.condition: Per-session listener accuracies are not reported; the 80% figure pools all 3 sessions.
entries.quote: The speech synthesis approach we demonstrated here used training data from five and a half months prior to testing and produced similar results over 3 separate days of testing, with recalibration but no retraining in each session.

entries.text: Authors frame earlier ECoG synthesis as offline analysis of normal speakers, except Metzger et al.
entries.condition: Statement restricted to ECoG; the reference list does not include the same first author's 2021 closed-loop sEEG synthesis study.
entries.quote: These studies and others using intraoperative recordings have also supported the feasibility of producing synthetic speech from ECoG high-gamma responses, but these demonstrations were based on offline analysis of ECoG signals that were previously recorded in subjects with normal speech, with the exception of the work by Metzger et al.

entries.text: The reference list does not cite Angrick et al. 2021 (Communications Biology), the closed-loop sEEG speech synthesis study by the same first author; the closed-loop synthesis lineage cited is Guenther et al. 2009 (vowels) and Metzger et al. 2023.
entries.condition: Checked against the full reference list of the Version of Record.

entries.text: Target cites the same group's earlier result: the same participant controlled a communication board with ECoG speech-command decoding for 3 months without retraining or recalibration (Luo et al. 2023).
entries.condition: Command classification, not synthesis; same participant; described through the target's citation.
entries.quote: More recently, we showed that the same clinical trial participant could control a communication board with ECoG decoding of self-paced speech commands over a period of 3 months without retraining or recalibration.

entries.text: Target describes Metzger et al. as synthesizing sentences from silent speech attempts in a cued setting in a participant with anarthria.
entries.condition: Described through the target's citation; [concurrent] work.
entries.quote: More recently, Metzger et al. demonstrated in a clinical trial participant diagnosed with quadriplegia and anarthria a multimodal speech-neuroprosthetic system that was capable of synthesizing sentences in a cued setting from silent speech attempts.

entries.text: Authors chose delayed rather than simultaneous auditory feedback in anticipation of deteriorating speech.
entries.condition: Design rationale; no simultaneous-feedback condition was run.
entries.quote: We chose to provide delayed rather than simultaneous auditory feedback in anticipation of ongoing deterioration in the patient’s speech due to ALS, with increasing discordance and interference between actual and BCI-synthesized speech.

entries.text: Per-session (per-day) listener accuracies are not reported; only the pooled 80% and per-listener range are given.
entries.condition: Sec. Results, Synthesis performance and Fig. 2 checked.

entries.text: No comparison with a word classifier on the same six keywords (for example classification followed by playback of a recorded token) is reported.
entries.condition: Single-system evaluation; see t61.

entries.text: Overall listener accuracy for synthesized words was 80%.
entries.condition: 21 listeners, six-choice identification, samples from 3 closed-loop sessions after exclusions.
entries.quote: Overall, human listeners achieved an accuracy score of 80%, indicating that the majority of synthesized words could be correctly and reliably recognized.

entries.text: Listeners recognized almost all of the participant's natural spoken keyword samples.
entries.condition: Same six keywords, natural speech samples mixed into the same listening test.
entries.quote: In contrast, when tested on the participant’s natural speech, our human listeners correctly recognized almost all samples of the 6 keywords (99.8%).

entries.text: Angrick et al. 2021: closed-loop real-time synthesis from sEEG depth electrodes in one participant; audio not yet intelligible.
entries.condition: One epilepsy patient with stereotactic depth electrodes; imagined and whispered speech; real-time frame-level synthesis.
entries.quote: While reconstructed audio is not yet intelligible

entries.text: Angrick et al. 2021 generated audible speech in real time from stereotactic depth electrodes.
entries.condition: One participant; closed loop.
entries.quote: Using a participant implanted with stereotactic depth electrodes, we were able to reliably generate audible speech in real-time.

entries.text: Guenther et al. 2009: Kalman-filter decoding of attempted speech into formant parameters with auditory feedback within 50 ms.
entries.condition: One participant with locked-in syndrome from brainstem stroke; chronic Neurotrophic Electrode; vowel formant synthesis.
entries.quote: A Kalman filter-based decoder translated the neural signals generated during attempted speech into continuous parameters for controlling a synthesizer that provided immediate (within 50 ms) auditory feedback of the decoded sound.

entries.text: Guenther et al. 2009 participant had locked-in syndrome due to a brainstem stroke.
entries.condition: Chronic implant; single participant.
entries.quote: who suffers from locked-in syndrome due to a brain stem stroke

entries.text: Brumberg et al. 2018: EEG motor imagery controls a 2D formant vector synthesized in real time.
entries.condition: Scalp EEG, motor imagery, vowel formant synthesis.
entries.quote: synthesized in real-time for instantaneous auditory feedback

entries.text: Wairagkar et al. 2025: causal closed-loop voice synthesis within 10 ms from intracortical arrays.
entries.condition: One participant with ALS and severe dysarthria; intracortical arrays; closed loop.
entries.quote: We were then able to train a deep learning model that synthesized his intended voice in real-time by decoding his neural activity causally within 10 ms.

entries.text: Wairagkar et al. 2025: six-choice sentence matching accuracy of closed-loop synthesized speech.
entries.condition: Listeners match each of 956 sentences to one of 6 same-length sentence transcripts; median 100%.
entries.quote: The mean and median accuracies were 94.34% and 100%, respectively

entries.text: Wairagkar et al. 2025: open-transcription median WER of closed-loop synthesized speech.
entries.condition: Naive listeners, open transcription, closed-loop sentences.
entries.quote: The transcription median phoneme error rate (PER) was 34.00% and median word error rate (WER) was 43.75%.

entries.text: Wairagkar et al. 2026: listener transcription WER of synthesized voice, offline with simulated real-time inference.
entries.condition: Same participant and benchmark as Wairagkar 2025; offline evaluation with real-time inference simulation; preprint.
entries.quote: Naive human listeners transcribed brain2voice 2.0 synthesized voice with a word error rate of 5.24%

entries.text: Wairagkar et al. 2026 evaluated offline with simulated real-time inference.
entries.condition: Not a closed-loop result.
entries.quote: Model performance was assessed through offline evaluation with real-time inference simulation

entries.text: Anumanchipalli et al. 2019: listener transcription of synthesized sentences with word pools.
entries.condition: Offline ECoG synthesis, epilepsy participants, MTurk transcription with word pools.
entries.quote: Transcribed sentences had a median 31% WER with a 25-word pool size and 53% WER with a 50-word pool size.

entries.text: The medRxiv v1 abstract states that speech synthesis from intracranial signals had until then only been done in retrospective analyses of able-bodied epilepsy-surgery patients.
entries.condition: Preprint v1 abstract (2023-07-01), from api.biorxiv.org; the published version softened the wording; contradicted by online synthesis in Guenther 2009 (locked-in, chronic) and Angrick 2021 (online sEEG).
entries.quote: but until now this has only been done using retrospective analyses of recordings from able-bodied patients temporarily implanted with electrodes for epilepsy surgery

entries.text: The target's reference list cites Herff et al. 2016 EMBC (ECoG speech synthesis pilot) and Wairagkar et al. 2023 NER (intracortical synthesis from dorsal motor cortex).
entries.condition: Neither is in the wiki ledger; described through the target's citation and their abstracts/titles.
entries.quote: Towards direct speech synthesis from ECoG: A pilot study

entries.text: Wairagkar et al. 2023 NER cited by the target.
entries.condition: [concurrent] (2023-04-24); chronic intracortical, title only.
entries.quote: Synthesizing speech by decoding intracortical neural activity from dorsal motor cortex

entries.text: Authors state that longer longitudinal testing is needed to test stability explicitly.
entries.condition: Discussion.
entries.quote: Although longitudinal testing over longer time periods will be needed to explicitly test this, our findings provide additional support for the stability of ECoG as a BCI signal source for speech synthesis.

entries.text: Anumanchipalli et al. 2019 ran a closed-set word identification test with 10, 25 and 50 choices.
entries.condition: Offline ECoG synthesis, epilepsy participants, MTurk listeners.
entries.quote: We quantified the effect of word length (number of syllables) and the number of choices (10, 25, and 50 words) on speech intelligibility

entries.text: Kohler et al. 2022 ran a binary forced-choice listening test with 19 volunteers.
entries.condition: Offline sEEG synthesis, epilepsy patients.
entries.quote: we conducted a forced-choice listening test, in which healthy volunteers had to decide which one of two textual options a reconstructed audio was

entries.text: Herff et al. 2019 listeners chose among four options for the 30 best synthesized words.
entries.condition: Offline ECoG synthesis, awake craniotomy patients, 55 volunteers.
entries.quote: In the test, volunteers heard the 30 synthesized words with the highest spectral correlations and were given four options, the correct answer plus three distractors, to choose from.

entries.text: Herff et al. 2016: one-participant ECoG pilot resynthesizing audibly spoken speech in real time; feedback to the participant not stated.
entries.condition: Abstract only (Europe PMC); not in the wiki; implant type not stated in the abstract.
entries.quote: In this pilot study with one participant, we demonstrate that electrocoticography (ECoG) intracranial activity from temporal areas can be used to resynthesize speech in real-time.

entries.text: Littlejohn et al. 2025: online streaming large-vocabulary synthesis from high-density ECoG in a participant with anarthria, decoding in 80-ms increments.
entries.condition: Abstract only (Europe PMC); one clinical-trial participant with severe paralysis and anarthria; [later]; accuracy metrics not taken.
entries.quote: to achieve online large-vocabulary intelligible fluent speech synthesis personalized to the participant's preinjury voice with neural decoding in 80-ms increments

questions.q: Does this establish open-vocabulary speech synthesis for ALS?
questions.answer: No. The demonstration used overt speech from one participant and a closed six-keyword vocabulary; the authors explicitly say unseen-word synthesis was not achieved.

questions.q: What does the 80% intelligibility result measure, and what is its sample denominator?
questions.answer: It is human listener word-recognition accuracy in a six-choice test over samples from three online sessions. The paper reports 180 samples and exclusions, but not the exact scored denominator after the additional unquantified false-detection exclusions.

questions.q: How strong is the evidence for long-term stability?
questions.answer: Training preceded testing by about five and a half months; similar results were obtained on three separate days with recalibration but no retraining. The authors state that longer longitudinal testing is still needed.

questions.q: Can this approach work for silent speech or anarthria?
questions.answer: That was not demonstrated. Training used overt speech with aligned acoustic ground truth, and the authors say the current approach requires vocalization that may remain intelligible.

questions.q: Which reproducibility conditions require special attention?
questions.answer: The paper omits exact test/validation dates, model random seeds, and exact listener-test scoring denominator after exclusions. The replication script provides dates that conflict with training-script defaults, states training-only channel-selection statistics, and normalizes non-silence training audio to −3 dB.

questions.q: Version and first-public check: is the wiki text the target, and when was it first public?
questions.answer: Wiki text is the Version of Record (PMC11053081). First public as medRxiv 10.1101/2023.06.30.23291352 v1 on 2023-07-01 (only version). Prior < 2023-01; [concurrent] 2023-01 to 2024-01.

questions.q: Does the target cite the same first author's 2021 closed-loop sEEG synthesis, and are per-session accuracies reported? (writer, targeted passage check of the reference list and Results; reader route not used for these narrow checks)
questions.answer: No citation of Angrick et al. 2021 in the reference list; per-session accuracies are not reported, only the pooled 80% and per-listener range; Discussion says results were similar over 3 days.

questions.q: Triage 2026-11-27: participant type of the prior intracranial synthesis decoders, and the target's uncited/unledgered priors
questions.answer: 8 prior decoders verified in text as epilepsy-monitoring or awake-craniotomy recordings; Herff 2016 EMBC and Wairagkar 2023 NER found in the target's reference list (not in wiki); Herff 2016 classified from its abstract; Littlejohn 2025 from its abstract only.
